name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5
evidenceNote: Its proposed action rests on a single cell-culture enzyme test, and the only human data are small, uncontrolled studies of eye creams that also contain other active ingredients.
summary: A short peptide added to eye creams marketed for puffiness. Lab data are thin, human studies are small and uncontrolled, and the FDA does not approve cosmetics.
keyTakeaway: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is a short, four-amino-acid peptide sold to cosmetic makers under the trade name Eyeseryl and added to eye creams aimed at puffiness and dark circles. Its proposed action is blocking angiotensin-converting enzyme in the skin, which has been shown only in a cell-culture test. The human evidence is a 20-person, uncontrolled study of an eye cream that combined it with other actives, so its own contribution cannot be separated. The FDA does not approve cosmetics or their ingredients, so there is no FDA status to check.

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Proposed to inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing fluid buildup under the eyes; shown only in cell culture.

atGlance.label: Main uses
atGlance.value: Eye creams and serums marketed for puffiness, dark circles and fine lines.

atGlance.label: Topical form
atGlance.value: Applied to the skin in leave-on products, often alongside other peptides.

blocks.text: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is a synthetic chain of four amino acids with an acetyl group capping one end. It is a cosmetic ingredient, supplied to manufacturers under the trade name Eyeseryl, and it appears mainly in products for the delicate skin around the eyes [1][2].

Commercial eye creams that list it usually pair it with other cosmetic peptides, such as acetyl hexapeptide-8 (Argireline) and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, and market the blend for firmer eye contours, fewer fine lines, and less visible puffiness and dark circles [2]. It is not a medicine and is not taken by injection or by mouth.

Cosmetic peptides are usually grouped into signal peptides, carrier peptides, neurotransmitter-inhibiting peptides and enzyme-inhibiting peptides [3]. Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is described as an inhibitor of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), the same enzyme targeted by a class of blood pressure drugs. The theory is that blocking ACE in the skin reduces the leakiness of tiny blood vessels, which lets fluid drain from under the eyes and lessens swelling [1].

The direct evidence for that action is limited. A 2021 laboratory study tested five cosmetic peptides on human skin cells and measured ACE activity, finding an optimal concentration of acetyl tetrapeptide-5 for that effect in culture [4]. A result in cells grown in a dish does not show that a cream applied to the skin delivers enough of the peptide to the right place to change fluid balance.

Penetration is the central question for any topical peptide. A 2026 safety review by industry scientists summarized expert panel findings on several short cosmetic peptides, concluding that little if any crosses the skin into the body [3]. Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 was not among the peptides in that panel's reviews, so the same conclusion has not been formally reached for it [3].

No. Cosmetic ingredients are outside the FDA approval system: under US law, cosmetic products and their ingredients do not go through FDA approval before they are sold; color additives are the only exception. The FDA can still act against a cosmetic once it is on the market if it is unsafe or mislabeled [5].

What a company says about a product matters. The FDA decides whether something is a cosmetic or a drug by its intended use, judged largely from its claims. A product that promises to affect the structure or function of the body, or to treat a condition, is regulated as a drug [6]. That is why eye creams with this peptide speak of reducing the look of puffiness rather than treating fluid retention.

There are no published randomized, placebo-controlled trials of acetyl tetrapeptide-5 on its own. The human data come from studies of finished products. In one open-label study, 20 women aged 45 to 60 used an eye contour cream twice a day; the cream contained acetyl tetrapeptide-5 together with acetyl hexapeptide-3, a collagen-stimulating peptide and cross-linked hyaluronic acid [1].

rows: Crow's feet roughness measured by profilometry [1]
62% reported medium to very marked improvement

blocks.text: These figures show that the women's skin and their own ratings improved while using the cream. They cannot show what acetyl tetrapeptide-5 contributed, because there was no comparison group and the cream contained several actives. Ratings people give their own skin, when they know what they are using, are also prone to optimism.

The same 2021 cell study also tested peptide combinations that included acetyl tetrapeptide-5 against oxidative damage in skin cells, and one mixture reduced markers of that damage [4]. That supports further testing, not a conclusion about how a cream performs on a face.

No specific side effects of acetyl tetrapeptide-5 have been reported in the published studies, but those studies were small and short. Expert reviews of other short cosmetic peptides have found skin and eye irritation to be none to slight and no skin allergy, with products tolerated in studies lasting one to seven months [3].

Any leave-on product near the eyes can still irritate, often because of fragrance or preservatives rather than the active ingredient. Because ACE inhibition is the claimed mechanism, it is worth noting that there is no evidence of any effect on blood pressure from a topical cosmetic, and none would be expected if, as with similar peptides, very little is absorbed [3].
